You would think that they would have an improved anti-cheat after 14 years of gameplay but that is, unfortunately, not the case. This game can be fun but it can also be a dumpster fire wrapped in a train wreck.

If you're looking for a 5v5 shooter that can be fun with friends, then look no further. Just be prepared for terrible teammates, lots of hackers, and hundreds of wasted hours.

A Digital Love-Hate Relationship

Counter-Strike 2 delivers the most contrasting emotions imaginable. On one hand, dropping into a random match introduces you to wonderfully eccentric strangers whose identities remain a total mystery—players who tape their microphones to their mouths to chant prayers or casually vent their life stories.

Suddenly, the voice chat transforms into an impromptu stand-up comedy special, leaving you with an involuntary smile as hilarious, unscripted chaos unfolds. Executing a flawless site take with your team or pulling off a miraculous eco-round win simply wipes away all the stress of a long day.

The Other Side of the Coin

- The smooth, nostalgic feel of the CS:GO era sometimes feels missing; the movement and overall pacing don't quite capture that exact old-school flavor.

- Let's not ignore the reality of cheaters still occasionally slipping into lobbies despite Prime matchmaking, forcing you to question whether you just got outplayed or out-hacked.

Yet, despite all its flaws, head-scratching moments, and hacker frustrations, jumping in after a long day to share laughs and build camaraderie makes it all worth it. It’s deeply flawed, utterly maddening, but undeniably magnetic.

Author's Note: The purpose of this review is simply to bring a smile to anyone reading it, highlighting the game's lighthearted and fun side while acknowledging its genuine quirks. If you look at my profile and notice this account only picked up Prime in early 2024, don't worry—I'm no stranger to the franchise, having logged plenty of hours across CS 1.6 and CS:GO on older accounts. Good games, everyone!

Counter-Strike 2 – A 20+ Year Veteran’s Review

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike since late fall 2002. I fell in love with it immediately and spent weekend after weekend learning the game inside and out. I watched it grow into 1.6 — the version that, for a lot of people my age, still feels like the peak. I put years into it: new teammates, old teammates, LAN events, and countless hours both in and out of my free time because I genuinely loved the game.

When Source came out it was a rough adjustment. I understood that games need to evolve, so I gave it time and eventually got used to it, even while watching the Counter-Strike I originally fell in love with slowly change. Years later, CS:GO arrived. It was nothing like the game I’d known for over a decade, but I kept an open mind and eventually came to enjoy it on its own terms. The problem was that it never stopped changing. Patch after patch, the shift to free-to-play, systems and updates that most long-time players never asked for — the game kept moving further away from what made so many of us fall in love with it in the first place. It felt like it was being slowly buried under its own updates.

CS2 launched and I once again went in with an open mind. What I found was very little meaningful difference from CS:GO. The creative and structural vision that the original Counter-Strike developers had is gone. It feels like the same game is being recycled with a new label, wrapped in more cases, weapon finishes, ranking systems, and monetization layers. At that point I mostly stopped playing regularly. Now I log in maybe once every couple of weeks, sometimes once a month, because it feels like a shell of what I used to know.
I mainly play Dust 2. Because I don’t play often and rarely touch other maps, the ranking system has kept me in Silver for a long time. When I do play I’m usually at the top of the scoreboard. Recently I received a 20-hour VAC cooldown for “irregular gameplay” after using the Scout on Dust 2 during one of the rare days I actually got to play. From what I understand, the new VACNet system is flagging certain movement and weapon usage — including the Scout — as suspicious, even when no cheating is involved.

I’ve known cheaters have been a problem in this series since the beginning. Seeing Valve’s solution start hitting long-time players who simply play the way they’ve always played is a new low. After more than 20 years, this feels like another clear moment where the veteran player base is being pushed further to the side. I’ve been pretty patient with the changes over the years, but getting locked out of the game for a day because I used a Scout on Dust 2 on one of the few times I logged in is a step too far.

I still have a soft spot for Counter-Strike and I’ll probably come back again eventually. But Valve has spent years steadily alienating the players who stuck with the game the longest, and this is one of the clearest examples yet.

I tried deathmatch, only to get head-tapped by AKs with frame-perfect reactions. I read a bit and it turns out deathmatch/casual isnt good because its swarmed by bots running scripts to farm kills for experience and crates. Okay whatever I unlocked competitive, thats like the ranked thing isnt it? So I'll be able to play with people around my skill level? I won maybe one game out of a full fifteen, the one that I won was because the other team literally had a player disconnect, every other game wasn't close either, like blowouts every time. Read some more and it turns out the matchmaking is so poor that most games are completely one-sided, driven by one or two players playing several times better than anyone else farming kills, which was exactly my experience. Okay, dunno why its called competitive then, but someone in one of these games told me Premiere is probably more my speed. Awesome! Oh wait, nevermind, after a literal entire calendar day of playing Im only 30% of the way to unlocking that mode.

Practice isnt the solution, and saying otherwise is an excuse to offload the labor of onboarding new players. Everywhere I look I'm being told to "embrace the suck and practice", but practice modes with bots dont get me out of lobbies full of people that have been playing for a lifetime longer than I have and can hit frame-perfect AWP headshots in their sleep; And telling a new player "it sucks for the first hundred hours then you maybe get kinda good" feels braindead when the market for competitive shooters is as flooded as its ever been. There's a million options that respect my time, why choose the option that feels like it goes out of its way to be hostile?

A functioning match-making system to group the people that can hit frame-perfect AWP headshots and people like me separately shouldnt be beyond this billion-dollar corporation, or the game modes that provide that shouldnt be so separate. You can tell this game has been around for literal generations, and that the average player is a returning player. In loading in for the first time you're inundated with menus (and opportunities to purchase cosmetics, gross), with next to zero real explanation for what anything is. When you're designing a product under the assumption that the average user has been using it for a lifetime already, you dont think about new players. Thats exactly whats happened with this game, and you feel it every hour the game's running. It feels like I'm missing a thousand hours of context before I should even be able to launch.

⭐ RECOMMENDED: CS2 — A Masterpiece of Human Suffering

CS2 is genuinely one of the best games ever made. You launch it expecting a competitive shooter, but instead you get a psychological evaluation, an online casino, and a live demonstration of why humanity should never have discovered the internet.

The cheaters: Every third match feels like a job interview with someone who has a gaming chair sponsored by the devil himself. Bro is staring at walls, tracking enemies through seven dimensions, and still types "ez" after going 4–17. VAC is so effective that cheaters have time to get married, raise children, and teach their grandchildren how to use spinbot before receiving a ban.

The community: Absolutely beautiful. You miss one smoke and suddenly a 35-year-old Russian philosopher is explaining why your entire bloodline deserves execution. Teammates will flash you, block you, steal your weapons, and then report YOU for griefing. It's basically a family reunion, except everyone hates you and nobody brought a will.

The gambling addiction simulator: Why play the game when you can spend your rent money on a virtual knife? CS2 has successfully turned opening colorful rectangles into a financial strategy. You spend $100 on cases, receive $2 worth of digital garbage, and convince yourself the next one will change your life. Congratulations, you've recreated the financial crisis, except your bank account is being managed by a spinning animation.

The developers: Are they still alive? Does Valve employ actual human beings, or is CS2 maintained by three raccoons in a trench coat? Major issues can survive longer than entire civilizations. Meanwhile, a minor exploit that lets players have fun gets patched faster than a terminal cancer diagnosis. At this point, the dev team has the work ethic of a skeleton in a retirement home.

The chicken pet: And then there's the chicken. A chicken that contributes more to the emotional well-being of the community than the entire development team. It doesn't cheat, doesn't scream slurs into the microphone, doesn't gamble away its savings, and doesn't blame you for losing a 1v5. Honestly, the chicken deserves to be the next CEO of Valve. Give it a desk, a salary, and access to the update button. The game might actually improve.

The matchmaking: You get matched with people who have never seen a keyboard before, while the enemy team consists of five retired professional players who apparently share one collective brain cell dedicated exclusively to destroying your happiness. Your rank isn't a measure of skill. It's a measurement of how much psychological damage you can endure before becoming a missing-person case.

The final verdict: 10/10 if you're a masochist. 0/10 if you value your mental health, finances, relationships, or will to live.

The game is completely free-to-play, and that, combined with the massive graphical upgrade, is the main reason for this positive review of CS2. Everything that came out after "Counter-Strike: Source" was absolute garbage to me, but CS2 finally looks up to date, costs nothing, and completely caught my attention visually.
Of course, the gameplay takes some getting used to. The movement feels a bit more sluggish at first, and this miserable sub-tick system causes occasional debates because it changes the whole feel of the game. It still leads to situations where shots don't register properly or you die even though you were already safely behind a wall on your own screen. But once you get used to the new rhythm, you realize what a modern masterpiece the game has become visually.
Then there is the endless cheater problem, where you just hope Valve will clamp down harder soon. People cheat way more subtly nowadays compared to the old days—using stuff like silent aim, legit bots, or soft aim, not to mention the config cheaters who abuse settings for an unfair advantage. New players even have to buy Prime just to get a rank. Luckily, I got Prime status for free because I’ve been around for over 10 years and experienced basically 5 to 10 different Counter-Strike versions. But let’s be honest: even Prime barely protects you from cheaters on the official servers these days, as Valve simply can't get a grip on their system. So you only have the advantage because, as a veteran, you didn't have to burn money for it.
With all the hype around skins and loot boxes, they are really trying to milk people for their money these days. Looking back at the early days of CS 1.0, you still remember downloading skins for free from fan homepages. Fortunately, you don't have to participate in this modern cash grab to still have fun on the server thanks to the new engine and graphics.
In the end, I recommend it purely for the new visuals and because it's free. As a veteran, you definitely need thick skin because of the cheaters, but after the first 20.9 hours, the graphics simply hooked me again.

Counter-Strike 2 is a monumental visual and technical overhaul of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, preserving the legendary tactical gameplay while modernizing the platform on Valve’s Source 2 engine.

What Works
Sub-Tick Architecture & Shooting: The moving past 64-tick/128-tick server limits means input response, shooting, and grenade throws execute instantly regardless of tick rate, making gunplay feel razor-sharp once adapted.

Dynamic Volumetric Smoke: Smokes now interact dynamically with lighting, bullets, and HE grenades. Blowing a temporal hole through a smoke wall with a grenade creates entirely new tactical dynamics and outplay opportunities.

Source 2 Visuals & Audio: Overhauled maps feature realistic PBR materials, clear reflections, improved lighting, and readable sightlines. The directional audio rework significantly improves sound localization.

Quality-of-Life Upgrades: Features like weapon refunds during buy phases, customizable loadout menus, and a transparent Premier ranking ladder streamline the competitive experience.

Room for Improvement
Anti-Cheat Concerns: Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC) still struggles to consistently filter out cheaters in high-ELO Premier matches compared to third-party platforms like FACEIT.

Content Parity: Missing legacy game modes, custom community map features, and server browser integrations from CS:GO are still being built back out.

Optimization & Frame Pacing: Higher hardware requirements mean lower-end PCs may experience performance dips or frametime spikes compared to legacy CS:GO.

The Verdict
CS2 lays an exceptional technical foundation for the next decade of competitive FPS games. While it launched with some content gaps, its core dynamic systems and graphical polish deliver the premier tactical shooter experience available today.
